awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Recycling Wind Turbine Blades into Construction Materials
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the development of a technology to recycle wind turbine blades into reinforced construction materials. The technology leverages advanced fiber-spinning techniques to process turbine blade waste into layered fibers with optimized mechanical and chemical properties. Unlike conventional recycling methods that degrade material quality, this technology preserves and enhances the fibers' structural integrity, making them suitable for high-performance applications in construction. The technology may provide an effective solution to waste management while enhancing the mechanical properties of construction composites to meet industry standards for strength, fire resistance, and sustainability. The aim of the lab to market translation is to integrate wind turbine fibers into commercial building materials such as concrete.  This technology may be a scalable and cost-effective solution for wind turbine blade recycling.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a fiber-spinning process that transforms decommissioned wind turbine blades into high-performance reinforcement fibers for sustainable construction materials. The increasing number of retired wind turbine blades presents a growing environmental challenge, as current disposal methods, such as landfilling and incineration, are costly and unsustainable. This technology seeks to address this issue by converting turbine blade waste, particularly glass-fiber-reinforced polymer composites, into valuable fibers that enhance the mechanical strength, thermal resistance, and durability of building materials. The technology uses advanced fiber spinning techniques to recycle wind turbine blade waste into coaxial layered fibers with enhanced mechanical and functional properties, intended for high-performance, sustainable applications in construction and energy management. Multilayered fibers are developed with a three-phase spinneret, which then may be integrated into biomass (e.g., hemp) concrete, enhancing durability, thermal resistance, fire retardance, and soundproofing. By incorporating these recycled fibers, the technology may reduce landfill waste and promote energy-efficient construction.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report

Award Title: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Recycling Wind Turbine Blades into Construction Materials

Federal Award ID: 2507116

Wind energy is an important component of the transition toward sustainable energy production. However, the increasing number of decommissioned wind turbine blades presents a significant waste management challenge. These blades are primarily composed of glass-fiber-reinforced polymer composites that are difficult to recycle using conventional methods. Existing recycling approaches often produce low-value materials or require energy-intensive processing, limiting the economic viability of recycling. This NSF I-Corps project investigated the commercial potential of an innovative fiber manufacturing technology that transforms wind turbine blade waste into high-performance composite fibers for construction and other industrial applications.

The underlying technology uses advanced coaxial and multilayer fiber-spinning processes to incorporate mechanically recycled wind turbine blade materials into engineered polymer fibers. By controlling the distribution and orientation of recycled glass fibers within the polymer matrix, this approach offers opportunities to improve material performance while recovering value from industrial waste. Previous research demonstrated improvements in mechanical properties, structural organization, and thermal stability, establishing the scientific foundation for exploring commercial applications.

During the award period, the project focused on translating this laboratory-developed technology toward practical industrial use through the NSF I-Corps customer discovery and entrepreneurial training process. The team investigated the needs of potential customers and stakeholders across wind energy, composite recycling, advanced manufacturing, construction materials, and sustainable infrastructure. These activities helped the team examine potential commercial applications, understand industry requirements, and identify barriers that must be addressed before the technology can be adopted at a commercial scale.

The project also supported engagement with industrial collaborators and potential commercialization partners, including TPI Composites, 123dtechs, Pure Shenandoah, and Advanced Functional Fabrics of America (AFFOA). These relationships provided a foundation for exploring feedstock availability, manufacturing scalability, product development, and potential industrial applications. In particular, the project considered opportunities to transform recycled wind turbine blade materials into reinforcement fibers for construction composites, including cementitious and bio-based building materials, while also exploring the broader potential of multilayer composite fibers for advanced manufacturing.

Intellectual Merit: The project advanced understanding of the translation potential of architected composite fiber manufacturing by connecting scientific innovation with industrial requirements and market needs. The I-Corps process helped identify important technical and commercialization questions, including feedstock variability, manufacturing consistency, processing costs, material performance, product qualification, and scalability. These findings provide direction for future research and development aimed at moving the technology beyond laboratory demonstrations toward commercially relevant manufacturing processes.

Broader Impacts: The project contributes to efforts to reduce industrial waste, promote resource efficiency, and develop sustainable manufacturing technologies. By investigating pathways to convert decommissioned wind turbine blades into value-added products, the technology has the potential to reduce reliance on landfilling while creating opportunities for domestic manufacturing, sustainable construction, and economic development. The project also supported entrepreneurial education and strengthened connections among academic researchers, small businesses, and industrial stakeholders.

Overall, the NSF I-Corps award established a foundation for the next stage of technology translation. The outcomes will inform future research, pilot-scale manufacturing, industrial validation, and commercialization activities aimed at transforming wind turbine blade waste into high-performance engineered materials. The project demonstrates how federally supported scientific discoveries can be connected with market needs to support innovation, environmental sustainability, and the development of new manufacturing opportunities in the United States.
